problem:
Consider the set of matrices ${A,B,C},$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 
If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}$ from a non-zero solution of ${x}_{1}A+{x}_{2}B+{x}_{3}C=O,$ where $O$ is the $2\times 2$ zero-matrix.

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Coefficients That Show Linear Dependence Among Matrix Vectors
examples.problem:
Consider the set of matrices $\big\{A, B \big\},$ where 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\dfrac{x_1}{x_2}$ from a non-zero solution of $x_1A+x_2B=O,$ where $O$ is the $2 \times 2$ zero-matrix.
examples.worked_solution:
If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist $x_1,x_2$ not both zero such that 

$$
x_1A+x_2B=O.
$$

Otherwise, if $x_1 = x_2 = 0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the matrices $A$ and $B$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -6\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & 0 \\ -2{x}_{1} & 4{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} & 5{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} & -6{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} & 5{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} & 4{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+(-4){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & -18 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{8}{5}){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+\frac{18}{5}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. Therefore, we get the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{2}=0,\end{aligned}
$$

which has only the zero solution $x_1=x_2=0.$

Consequently, $\big\{A, B \big\}$ is linearly independent.

feedback.problem:
Consider the set ${{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)}$ of polynomials from $R[t],$ where

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=3-2{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=-6+4{t}^{2}.
$$

If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}}$ from a non-zero solution of ${x}_{1}\cdot {p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}\cdot {p}_{2}(t)=0.$
feedback.worked_solution:
If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ not both zero such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)=0.
$$

Otherwise, if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the given expressions for ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t)$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(3-2{t}^{2})+{x}_{2}(-6+4{t}^{2}) & =0 \\ (3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2})+(-2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}){t}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation is true for every $t$ if and only if 

$$
{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot column is the $1$st one. Hence, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the $1$st equation, we get

$$
3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, for any ${x}_{2}\ne 0,$ we obtain 

$$
\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2{x}_{2}}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$
